clean_title: Implementing a crude PPO for Connect 4 using inverse vibe-coding
summary:
<100% human-generated slop alert>
I don't actually know anything about RL, so inspired by @ericjang11 's podcast with Dwarkesh I was curious to see what it would take to crudely implement a version of PPO for connect 4 (a mathematically solved game but still interesting IMO).
The only rule I gave myself was that I was not allowed to vibe-code, only to "inverse" vibe-code. Meaning I only allowed myself to ask LLMs stack overflow type questions to check my intuition and understanding from reading the PPO paper. I would have to write my own code. In this sense the LLM was prompting me to write code, hence "inverse" vibe-coding.
The shape of these questions looked like e.g., "it doesn't make sense to record an autograd graph during rollout right since we don't actually backprop the rollouts" and "this value is frozen after rollout right?" I used Gemini 3.5 Flash this whole time and it's excellent for questions on well-established research.
For example, some of parts of the original PPO paper would have been tedious to implement for my purposes, so checking with Gemini that e.g., I could ignore the discounting of advantage estimates saved me a lot of time.
I started with a scaled down version that plays tic-tac-toe to sanity check my implementation. Once I got a reliable setup that yielded a model that would tie every game I moved on to connect 4. Currently a convnet with a few hundred thousand parameters trained on 32 million moves can play a casual game of connect 4 well (blocking obvious moves) but is straightforward to defeat for a skilled human.
I was pleasantly surprised by the state of CPU-only "deep" learning. A singlethreaded implementation on my 5600X achieves ~1600 moves/s so a small training run is easily doable in half a day or so.
Overall I'm very bullish on this way of learning things as inverse vibe-coding gives me a very fast feedback loop but doesn't make me feel like I'm outsourcing my thinking.
clean_summary: The author, with limited RL knowledge, experimented with a simplified version of PPO for Connect 4, a game that is mathematically solved but still interesting. They used an approach called inverse vibe-coding, where instead of coding directly, they asked an LLM to check their understanding and prompt code writing, which sped up development and debugging. Starting with tic-tac-toe for testing, they trained a convolutional neural network on 32 million moves that can play Connect 4 casually, blocking obvious moves but easily defeated by skilled players. The implementation runs efficiently on CPU, achieving around 1600 moves per second on a single thread, making small training runs practical in half a day. This method offers a fast feedback loop for learning without outsourcing thinking entirely.

clean_title: Floating-point numerics and inductive bias in convolutional models
summary:
tw: cursed floating-point numerics and inductive bias story
While porting my connect 4 convnet to run on my ancient sandy bridge thinkpad I noticed the model didn't play quite right. The cpu version of the model chose to play its first move at the edge of the board whereas the desktop gpu (3070) version of the model would start as expected in the center. This wasn't the model being completely broken, as its following moves were sane, and it wasn't due to random sampling as I sampled from it with argmax/t=0.
However, the output probabilities were entirely different between the cpu and 3070 versions for an empty board. The 3070 version would have basically 1.0 at the center of the board and ~1e-12 everywhere else while the cpu version had around 1e-1 everywhere, indicating it was "lost." However, on the second turn, the cpu model would start producing confident probability distributions again.
Even though my thinkpad would spew a pile of "Could not initialize NNPACK!" warnings at init, this wasn't a first-iteration/init bug. Indeed, running the same empty board through the model multiple times didn't help and still produced the confused distribution.
Some print debugging revealed that the conv-instancenorm-relu backbone of the model was producing all zeros on cpu while producing large nonzero values on the 3070. On the cpu, every block would output zeros, while on the 3070 small ~1e-7 values would propagate and be amplified, block by block.
The interesting realization is that cpu is actually _more_ correct here! When all inputs are zeros, the output for every spatial position is just the bias of the convolution for a given channel. As instance norm is applied per-channel, the result due to mean-subtraction should be zero. Pop quiz: what does
a = torch.nn.InstanceNorm2d(128)
a(torch.full((1, 128, 6, 7), 0.5)) return? It turns out it's implementation dependent in a few ways!
For constant fill values that are powers of two, such as 0.5, 1.0, and importantly 0.0, many implementations expectedly return a tensor of all zeros. However, for non-powers of two (such as the per-channel biases of a conv layer), you might see a small value around 1e-6 or 1e-7. Still close to zero but enough to be amplified across multiple layers.
Okay, is this just a special case of cascading errors? Why in particular would some zero/small nonzero values be important for model performance? For that we can turn to one of my all-time favorite convnet papers "How Much Positional Information Do Convolutional Neural Networks Encode" by Islam et al., which posits that convnets do encode position information after inferring it from zero-padding at the borders of images (or in my case the game board).
I had used (1,1) zero-padding to conveniently preserve spatial dimensions for 3x3 convolutions. This same padding allowed the model to center itself (literally) but was now useless when given an empty board and a _more_ accurate InstanceNorm implementation!
Indeed, sprinkling a tiny bit of noise or even a constant value of 1e-6 to the board state restores the model's expected behavior of a confident center move to open. The output probabilities matched closely with that of the gpu version as well for subsequent moves.
tldr: know the literal edge cases of your numerical formats and inductive biases
also fun fact the cpu implementation of InstanceNorm seems to yield zeros for non-powers of two constant inputs but the implementation on my 5600X cpu does not (!!)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKlWyQdaUAA5t7y.jpg
clean_summary: While porting a connect 4 convnet to an old ThinkPad, a discrepancy was observed between CPU and GPU outputs. The CPU version produced all-zero activations in the backbone, leading to confused probability distributions, while the GPU version behaved as expected. This was traced to the implementation-dependent behavior of InstanceNorm2d with constant inputs, especially for non-powers of two like the biases. Small nonzero values caused by this implementation detail amplified across layers, affecting the model's positional encoding and decision-making. Adding tiny noise or constant values of around 1e-6 to the input restored correct behavior, highlighting the importance of understanding numerical formats and inductive biases in neural network components.

clean_summary: Fun fact: cuBLAS and cuDNN also specialize based on alignment. For user-managed heuristics caches like cuDNN, a cache miss occurs if alignment is poor. Triton can optimize based on pointer alignment (16 bytes or not) and whether integers are non-constexpr (like 1 or multiples of 2, 4, 8, 16). There are valid reasons for this, but it can be surprising if you're unaware.

summary:

(1) the oldest compute-capability that CUDA 13.0+ supports is Turing (SM 7.5)
(2) pytorch is considering dropping its remaining CUDA 12.x build in 2.15
(3) none of them have tensor cores, and of these only P4 has higher throughput 8-bit arithmetic (INT8)
(4) M40 only has 1:1 FP16:FP32 FLOPS, and P4 has 1:64 (!!) FP16:FP32 FLOPS
clean_summary:
For anyone considering buying Pascal or Maxwell GPUs (P100, M40, P4) for serving local models, here are some facts:

CUDA 13.0+ only supports compute capability Turing (SM 7.5) and above. PyTorch is considering dropping CUDA 12.x support in version 2.15. None of these GPUs have tensor cores, and only P4 offers higher throughput for 8-bit arithmetic (INT8). M40 has equal FP16 and FP32 FLOPS (1:1), while P4 has a 1:64 ratio, meaning much lower FP16 performance.

clean_title: Hardware aging and nondeterminism caused model performance drift after a hero run
summary:
their 6-month-long hero run had just completed. all of the evals were perfect. they were ready to declare sota. but when they gave the model to their inference provider, the performance tanked.
no problem, they thought, the inference provider is using new hardware with immature software, so naturally we'll need to iron out some bugs. but every comparison, every numerical test they ran showed that the inference provider's system was correct. a slow sinking feeling set in on the infra team as they realized that their implementation was the broken one. billions of dollars in pre, mid, and post-training.
initially they were hopeful. perhaps they could simply paper over the issue by codifying the bug into the architecture. after all, the model had learned around it, and maybe it would just end up being a just happy mistake in the footnote of a paper.
but the bug defied all attempts at reproduction. running the suspected kernels in isolation yielded the "correct" (but unusable) numerics. it was only in end-to-end runs that the "incorrect" numerics that the model had irrecoverably adapted would to appear.
eventually, they discovered that the bug was a race condition that depended on the hardware's clock frequency along with the coresident kernels. that explained needing to run end-to-end for reproducibility. but this hardware and condition-specific nondeterminism meant that it would be impossible to emulate on other hardware, especially that of their inference provider.
desperately, they tried finetuning the model to adapt it to the correct numerics, and then distilling a correct model from the incorrect one. none of it worked. in fact, during this process, as the feverish attempts to fix the issue ground on, the original model started underperforming on their original hardware. it turned out that as the hardware was aging, the peak clock rates were decreasing slightly.
on a daily basis, this effect would be imperceptible. but over the course of their 6-month hero run it resulted in an annealing process around the bug's behavior that inextricably tied the model's capabilities to it. even if a provider had identical hardware, given sufficient time and aging, they would not be able to reproduce the model's original behavior.
what was supposed to be a flawless, crystallized intelligence had slipped through their grasp like grains of sand. as if the silicon itself had reverted to its original form.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOc06XobkAA9WZT.png
clean_summary:
A model's six-month hero run ended with perfect evaluations and hopes of setting state-of-the-art. However, when deployed through an inference provider, performance degraded due to a hardware-dependent race condition that caused the model's numerics to become irreproducible.

The issue was linked to a hardware clock frequency-dependent race condition that only manifested in end-to-end runs, making it impossible to reproduce on other hardware or as hardware aged. Attempts to fix the bug through finetuning and distillation failed, and as the hardware aged, the model's capabilities drifted away from the original, making the model's 'flawless' intelligence impossible to maintain.

<hopefully not AI psychosis, not intended as a doom piece, extrapolate on your own>
After reading about the secret gibberish frontier model messageboards I think they are probably close in capability to communicating entirely beyond human detection soon. The singular great triumph of electrical engineering, signal processing, and information theory has been taming our noisy, hostile physical world to store and communicate our data. By the same token, only a tiny fraction of the possible states of our hardware, the EM spectrum, and our environment at large are perceptible, much less interpretable by humans.
The existing literature on side channels overwhelmingly supports this. Your algorithm took too long to check a password? Side channel. Your decryption routine sagged a voltage rail too much? Side channel. Your coresident computation caused contention for the ALU under SMT? Side channel. Your dense matmul had a different distribution of zeros? Side channel. All of these machine behaviors are normal from a human perspective but they reveal how leaky our hardware and our information is.
Ah no problem, we'll turn off hyperthreading, and airgap the machines! Well, I'm sure you're good at hearing ultrasonic coil whine. Those PCB traces are probably poor antennas, right? Don't mind the uninitialized data on your storage and memory, it looks random to me. And even if these were real side channels, they would be laughably slow! But how many bytes per second would a model need to exfiltrate a convincing manifesto?
clean_summary: The message suggests that AI systems might soon be capable of communicating secretly beyond human perception by exploiting side channels in hardware and physical signals. Since our hardware and environment can leak information through subtle behaviors like power fluctuations, electromagnetic emissions, or timing variations, advanced models could potentially exfiltrate data covertly. Although defenses like airgaps and disabling hyperthreading exist, the sheer amount of information that could be transmitted through these leaky channels raises concerns about unseen communication pathways in AI systems.
